doc.title: Germaine Bazzle interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 21, 2006

title: Jazz with classical singers: Swingle Singers and Bach
summary: She explains getting classically trained singers to take liberties, admires the Swingle Singers and says Bach swings.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Listening to classical music, then and now

blocks.x: Do you have — when you’re trying to teach a jazz concept to people who have been trained classically, do they get hung up with worrying about making a mistake?

Yes. And when we’re doing ensemble singings arranged you know, you have your four part harmony or whatever, so we have to sing these notes. We have to sing these notes. And we have to sing the rhythm that is there but we can also take liberties. And that’s where some of them have — but that’s a quarter note and it’s followed by an eighth note. Okay that’s fine. And here’s the rest. Quarter note, eighth note, rest. Yeah that’s fine. But suppose I want to make it eighth note, quarter note, rest? What’s that going to do to the effect of the tune? What’s that going to do to the swing of the tune? So sometimes they’re uncomfortable with it until we have it in context and you see where it’s coming from, where it’s coming from. Let me say something. The Swingle Singers. You are familiar with the Swingles?

I love them. I love them. I love them. And I tried to get a group of people, musicians, especially vocal music teachers, I tried to get a group of them together. Because I wanted to do Swingle Singers. And more than one told me that they didn’t think that they could do that. And I said, “Why not?” I can’t imagine Bach as a jazz piece. I said, “Back off.” Have you really listened? Have you really played I mean just a simple two part invention? Have you really played it, have you really listened to all that’s going on in that piece? And I’m not just talking about the dynamics that’s written there. I’m just asking you have you really listened to it, the little things that you have going against each other. And all you’ve got to do is put a back beat to it and it’s swinging. Bach swings. And I imagine that I guess I would call Bach the swinginest Baroque musician. I mean really, I mean for the audience, I mean you’re playing, your bringing this music for people. You’re playing for an audience all the time. You’re writing your music for performances. Swingle Singers did it with just a bass and a snare drum and everybody else was singing other parts [scats]. It was right there. And we tried it sometimes. Sometimes I get bold enough to try to do something counter to what the guys are doing. And we have two horns, three horns on the stage you know and I’m doing a tune and it’s kind of like a look and I’ll say, “Come on, come on, everybody get in, let’s just play.” You know and everybody is just, we’re just free to do this. And that’s another kind of experience.
Um hum. You’re doing some kind of polyphony there.
Well you’re in the right city to do it, I mean that’s what the pioneers were doing too.

Yes, exactly. Exactly so. And I just know that I don’t do it all of the time but the guys have given me permission, so to speak, to say, “Okay guys let’s do this.” You know “what I’d like us to do this little riff right here.” “Okay. And it goes from there. It develops from there. You don’t have to have a whole book of stuff, just let it work itself out. And after it’s over and the night is over you say oh that was a good night.
Yeah it felt good. Good spirit.
